content: They also worked to clarify the language, particularly regarding implementation and how policymakers and program staff might interpret the recommendations. No additional recommendations were solicited from the External Peer Review Group. The WHO Steering Committee compiled the feedback from the External Peer Review Group and collaborated with the chairs to address any inconsistencies or contradictions. Acknowledgments were provided for the members of the Guideline Development Group, representing various countries and disciplines, along with their affiliations. All members of the Guideline Development Group, systematic review teams, and the External Peer Review Group were required to declare any conflicts of interest before participating in meetings. The WHO Steering Committee reviewed these declarations to determine if any conflicts might limit or preclude participation. No conflicts of interest requiring action were identified, but all declared potential conflicts were summarized. For example, Lesley Bamford, an employee of the National Department of Health in South Africa, declared her public position on breastfeeding as outlined in the Tshwane Declaration. She advocates for and defends this position as part of her role. It was agreed that she could fully participate in the deliberations and decision-making. Similarly, Louise Kuhn disclosed her involvement in projects related to breast milk oligosaccharides, cytokines, early antiretroviral therapy in neonates, and follow-up of children living with HIV, funded by various U.S. institutions. She was also allowed to fully participate. Angela Mushavi, employed by the Elizabeth Glaser Pediatric AIDS Foundation and seconded to Zimbabwe’s Ministry of Health, declared her role in coordinating services for preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission and promoting breastfeeding as a child survival strategy. She was also permitted full participation. Anju Seth, a co-investigator on a UNICEF-funded project addressing the nutritional needs of children affected by HIV, declared her involvement, and it was agreed she could fully participate. The Guideline Development Group used the GRADE method to evaluate the quality of evidence. This standardized approach assesses evidence quality and distinguishes it from the strength of recommendations. GRADE tables summarized study details, including outcomes, limitations, inconsistencies, indirectness, imprecision, and other factors affecting evidence quality. Members then categorized the overall evidence quality as very low, low, moderate, or high. Evidence from randomized controlled trials was generally rated as high quality, while observational studies were rated lower. Adjustments to these ratings were made based on factors such as study limitations, consistency, directness, precision, and potential biases. For each draft recommendation, the WHO Steering Committee presented a synthesis of evidence, GRADE tables, and draft recommendation language. Decision-making tables were drafted to evaluate the benefits and risks of interventions, the values and preferences of mothers living with HIV and their communities, and the feasibility of implementation, particularly in resource-limited settings. Members independently reviewed the material, provided comments, and suggested revisions. They also assessed the evidence quality, the balance of benefits versus harms, and the applicability of recommendations to target populations. The strength of recommendations was categorized as strong, conditional, or requiring further research. Strong recommendations indicated confidence that the benefits outweighed the risks, making them suitable for adoption as policy in most situations. Conditional recommendations were more context-specific, requiring further stakeholder involvement and debate before adoption. In cases where evidence was insufficient, no recommendation was made, and further research was deemed necessary. Consensus-building was central to finalizing recommendations. If consensus could not be reached, a majority vote was used to resolve contested decisions. WHO staff facilitated discussions but did not express personal opinions on the data or decisions. All recommendations were agreed upon after revisions, with extensive discussions on breastfeeding duration for mothers living with HIV to achieve consensus on recommendation strength. The recommendations will be disseminated through WHO’s network of international partners, including country and regional offices, health ministries, collaborating centers, and NGOs. They will also be published on the WHO website and partner agency platforms. Efforts will be made to adapt the guidelines to national contexts, considering local social, cultural, and economic factors. Stakeholder discussions will inform decision-making on implementation, and frameworks like DECIDE will be shared to assist policymakers. Monitoring and evaluation will be integral to implementation, focusing on strong recommendations. National child health programs will collect and report data on pregnant women and mothers living with HIV and their exposed newborns. Key areas for monitoring include infant feeding practices, ART coverage among mothers, and growth outcomes in breastfed infants. WHO will track guideline implementation through requests for technical assistance, monitoring and evaluation support, and downloads of the guideline publication. Future research priorities include clinical and programmatic questions identified during discussions. Implementation research will support policy adoption and enable effective implementation. Small-scale demonstration projects may aid in scaling up training and capacity development. The guideline will be reviewed in 2019, with updates made as needed based on new evidence or urgent findings.
